results.result: Through iterative laboratory evolution and rational engineering, three mutations (pgi H386Y, crp H22N, rpoB A1245V) are sufficient for E. coli to grow autotrophically when combined with heterologous carbon-fixing and energy modules. This was determined by identifying consensus mutations across multiple evolved lineages, introducing them into ancestor strains, and demonstrating essentiality through reversion experiments.
results.evaluation: The iterative approach combining evolution (C27, C34) with rational engineering (C30, C36) is well-documented. Essentiality is demonstrated through reversion experiments (C33, C37) showing loss of phenotype when mutations are removed. The workflow systematically narrowed mutations from multiple evolved strains to a minimal set, with appropriate controls and validation at each step.

results.result: The compact autotrophic strain exhibits growth characteristics nearly identical to previously evolved autotrophic strains, with a doubling time of approximately 24 hours. 13C-labeling experiments confirm that all biomass carbon derives from CO2, validating complete autotrophic metabolism.
results.evaluation: Growth rate comparison (C41) is supported by Figure 2A with appropriate replicates (n=3). The 13C-labeling experiment (C42) provides direct evidence of carbon source through isotopic tracing, reaching expected labeling fractions after ~4 doublings. The doubling time calculation (C43) is derived from linear regression of growth data with clear methodology.

results.result: The pgi H386Y mutation reduces phosphoglucoisomerase activity approximately 100-fold (from ~130 s⁻¹ to ~1.5 s⁻¹), stabilizing the carbon-fixing cycle by reducing efflux from the autocatalytic rPP cycle. This results in a 3-fold increase in the F6P/G6P ratio and elevated levels of rPP cycle metabolites.
results.evaluation: The enzymatic activity measurements (C55, C56, C57) are performed with purified proteins using standard spectrophotometric assays (n=3), showing clear ~100-fold reduction. Metabolomics data (C58, C59) with LC-MS/MS support the predicted metabolic consequences. The mechanistic interpretation (C4) logically follows from the biochemical data and is consistent with autocatalytic cycle theory (C49).

results.result: The crp H22N and rpoB A1245V mutations cause widespread transcriptional changes including ~5-fold upregulation of fdoGH (formate dehydrogenase) and rpiB (ribose-phosphate isomerase B), alongside >4-fold downregulation of multiple catabolic operons (gat, ara, man) and amino acid biosynthesis pathways.
results.evaluation: Proteomics analysis compared evolved vs ancestor and double mutant vs wild-type strains under identical conditions (xylose-limited chemostat). Fold-changes are reported with statistical significance (p<0.05) and consistent patterns across independent comparisons (Figure 5). The epistatic effects between mutations (C78) are documented, though mechanistic understanding remains incomplete.

results.result: The crp H22N and rpoB A1245V double mutant exhibits a >20-fold increase in NADH/NAD+ ratio in the presence of formate, significantly higher than the ~10-fold increase in wild-type (p<0.05), with no significant difference in the absence of formate.
results.evaluation: The NADH/NAD+ measurements (C82, C83) are performed with appropriate replicates (n=6) using LC-MS/MS with 13C internal standards. Statistical significance is reported (p<0.05) and the formate-dependence (C84) provides important mechanistic context. The measurements are normalized to wild-type without formate, providing clear baseline comparison.

results.result: The double mutant (crp H22N, rpoB A1245V) expressing formate dehydrogenase shows >25% increase in final OD when grown with xylose and formate, but also exhibits >10 hour longer lag time. The yield increase is formate-dependent and not observed when grown on xylose alone.
results.evaluation: Growth experiments (C79, C80, C81) are documented in Figure 6A&B with clear formate-dependence. The increased yield with extended lag time presents an interesting phenotype, though the mechanistic basis remains speculative. The formate-dependence control (C81) strengthens the interpretation that the effect relates to energy module integration.

results.result: The autotrophy-enabling gene set (three mutations plus heterologous modules) is sufficient for autotrophic growth without auxiliary knockouts (ΔpfkA, ΔpfkB, Δzwf), though the resulting strain shows reduced performance (half the final OD and less than half the growth rate) compared to the strain with knockouts.
results.evaluation: While autotrophic growth without auxiliary knockouts is demonstrated (C45), an unintentional rrsA mutation was introduced during construction (C47), creating uncertainty about which genetic changes are truly necessary. The reduced growth performance (C46) is documented but the contribution of the rrsA mutation versus absence of knockouts cannot be distinguished. Additional controls without the rrsA mutation would be needed.

results.result: The autotrophy-enabling mutations achieve three main effects: (i) stabilizing the carbon-fixing cycle by reducing branch-point efflux, (ii) increasing NADH/NAD+ ratio through decoupled formate utilization via FDH-O, and (iii) improving resource allocation by downregulating unnecessary metabolic pathways.
results.evaluation: This integrative mechanistic model (C85) is supported by multiple lines of evidence: pgi activity reduction and metabolite changes (Result 3), NADH/NAD+ increase (Result 5), and proteomic downregulation patterns (Result 4). The FDH-O hypothesis (C90) is speculative but consistent with natural chemolithoautotrophs (C89). The resource allocation interpretation (C88) logically explains the observed downregulation patterns.

results.result: Metabolic rewiring through auxiliary knockouts can serve as a temporary 'metabolic scaffold' to direct evolution toward desired phenotypes, then be removed once the phenotype is achieved. This strategy may help avoid evolutionary dead-ends where heterologous genes are lost or inactivated.
results.evaluation: The metabolic scaffold concept (C48, C95, C96) is supported by the demonstration that auxiliary knockouts can be removed after evolution (Result 7), though with caveats about the rrsA mutation. The evolutionary dead-end problem (C97) is well-established knowledge. The proposed strategy (C98) is a logical extension, though presented as speculation for future work rather than a tested hypothesis.

results.result: During genetic engineering, unintentional mutations occurred in rpoB (A1245V), uhpT (Q7* stop codon), and yejG. Reversion experiments confirmed that yejG is not essential for autotrophy, while uhpT is likely a loss-of-function with no effect on the phenotype.
results.evaluation: The unintentional mutations are identified through whole genome sequencing (C32, C38). The yejG reversion experiment (C40) directly tests essentiality. The uhpT interpretation (C39) is reasonable given it's an early stop codon in a hexose transporter, unlikely to affect autotrophic growth. This demonstrates appropriate quality control in strain construction.

results.result: The crp H22N mutation affects position H22 in activation region 2 of Crp, previously shown to influence promoter specificity and rPP cycle integration. The rpoB A1245V mutation is located in the RNA polymerase core near DNA interaction sites and was previously documented in high-temperature adaptation.
results.evaluation: The structural locations (C61, C64) are documented in Figure 5 supplement 3. Prior literature support (C62, C63, C65) provides context for the mutations' potential effects. The general roles of Crp and RpoB (C60, C63) are well-established. This contextualizes the mutations within known protein structure-function relationships.

results.result: The study demonstrates metabolism's extreme malleability and capacity to switch trophic modes with very few mutations in laboratory timescales. Synthetic autotrophy in E. coli can now be achieved with only a few defined steps without requiring extensive evolution.
results.evaluation: This conclusion (C99, C102) is well-supported by the demonstration that only three mutations are sufficient (Result 1), the relatively rapid evolution timescale (C34: ~1 month vs >90 days), and the successful rational engineering approach. The claim represents a valid synthesis of the experimental findings and their implications for metabolic engineering.

results.result: Four consensus mutations (rpoB, pgi, pcnB, malT) were identified across three independently evolved autotrophic clones. However, rpoB, pcnB, and malT are commonly mutated in adaptive lab evolution experiments generally, suggesting limited specific relevance to autotrophy.
results.evaluation: The consensus mutation identification (C28) follows from sequencing multiple independent lineages. The interpretation that pcnB and malT are likely non-specific (C29) is supported by citation to ALE literature and led to appropriate focus on pgi. This demonstrates sound experimental logic in distinguishing adaptive from hitchhiker mutations.

results.result: Upregulated genes fdoG and fdoH encode subunits of the native formate dehydrogenase O complex involved in respiratory chain electron transfer. The upregulated rpiB is an inducible isoenzyme of the constitutive rpiA. Downregulated operons include gat (galactitol), ara (arabinose), and man (mannose) degradation pathways, plus starvation sensing proteins rspA and rspB.
results.evaluation: These claims (C66, C68, C71, C73-C75, C77) represent established biochemical knowledge about gene functions and metabolic pathways in E. coli. They provide necessary context for interpreting the proteomics results but are not novel findings of this study. The information is accurate and appropriately cited or represents standard microbiology knowledge.

results.result: The authors used iterative laboratory evolution to identify three mutations (pgi, crp, and rpoB) that are sufficient for E. coli to grow autotrophically when introduced alongside non-native carbon-fixing and energy modules. Through two rounds of evolution, they isolated evolved clones, identified consensus mutations, and systematically tested which mutations were essential by introducing them into engineered strains and performing reversion experiments.
results.evaluation: Both reviewers explicitly affirm this core finding. The first reviewer states the authors 'define a set of just three mutations that promote autotrophy' and the second reviewer confirms 'the authors identify mutations in three genes - pgi, rpoB, and crp - that allow cells to metabolise CO2.' No concerns are raised about the experimental approach or the identification of these mutations.

results.result: The pgi mutation (H386Y) reduces the enzyme's activity approximately 100-fold (from ~130 s⁻¹ to ~1.5 s⁻¹), thereby stabilizing the carbon-fixing cycle by capping a major branching flux. This was demonstrated through in vitro enzyme assays and metabolomics showing increased F6P to G6P ratios and higher levels of rPP cycle metabolites in the mutant.
results.evaluation: Both reviewers explicitly endorse this finding. The first reviewer states 'The authors make a convincing case that mutations in pgi are loss-of-function mutations that prevent metabolic efflux from the reductive pentose phosphate autocatalytic cycle.' The second reviewer similarly affirms 'The authors make a strong case that mutations in pgi are loss-of-function mutations that prevent metabolic efflux from the reductive pentose phosphate autocatalytic cycle.' No concerns are raised about the biochemical characterization or mechanistic interpretation.

results.result: The crp and rpoB mutations result in widespread transcriptional changes including down-regulation of several metabolic pathways (gat, ara, man operons, amino acid biosynthesis) and increased expression of genes associated with the carbon-fixing module (rpiB) and energy module (fdoGH), with epistatic effects between the two mutations observed in proteomics data.
results.evaluation: The reviewers explicitly acknowledge these findings as valuable contributions. The second reviewer notes 'The major addition to the paper is the proteomic analysis of single and double mutants of crp and rpoB. These new data provide clues as to the role of the crp and rpoB mutations in promoting autotrophic growth.' The first reviewer states the data 'suggest possible roles of mutations in two other genes - crp and rpoB,' indicating acceptance of the proteomics results even if mechanistic details remain speculative.

results.result: The crp and rpoB double mutant shows a significantly increased NADH/NAD+ ratio (>20-fold vs ~10-fold in wild-type) when grown with formate, along with >25% increase in final OD but longer lag time, with these effects dependent on formate presence.
results.evaluation: The reviewers accept these experimental findings as part of the proteomics and metabolomics characterization. The second reviewer states 'These new data provide clues as to the role of the crp and rpoB mutations in promoting autotrophic growth, which the authors discuss.' The data on NADH/NAD+ ratios and growth parameters are presented as evidence supporting the proposed mechanisms, and no concerns are raised about these measurements.

results.result: The compact autotrophic strain (with pgi, crp, and rpoB mutations) has growth parameters nearly identical to previously characterized autotrophic strains, with a doubling time of about 24 hours, and 13C labeling verified that all biomass carbon stems from CO2.
results.evaluation: The reviewers do not question these characterization data. The first reviewer acknowledges the study 'define[s] a set of just three mutations that promote autotrophy,' implicitly accepting the growth and labeling validation. The second reviewer confirms the authors successfully 'identify mutations in three genes...that allow cells to metabolise CO2,' accepting the functional validation of autotrophic growth.

results.result: The autotrophy-enabling gene set (pgi, crp, rpoB mutations) is sufficient to achieve autotrophic growth even without the auxiliary knockouts (zwf, pfkAB), though with reduced performance (half the final OD and less than half the growth rate), demonstrating that metabolic rewiring can serve as a temporary 'metabolic scaffold.'
results.evaluation: The reviewers do not challenge these findings about the sufficiency of the three mutations or the metabolic scaffold concept. The first reviewer's statement that the authors 'define a set of just three mutations that promote autotrophy' and emphasis on 'the malleability of E. coli metabolism' implicitly accepts these results. No concerns are raised about the experiments testing autotrophy without auxiliary knockouts.

results.result: The authors propose three main mechanistic effects of the mutations: (i) integrating the carbon fixation cycle by enhancing internal flux over outgoing flux via pgi, (ii) facilitating energy module integration by decoupling formate harvesting and increasing NADH/NAD+ ratio via crp/rpoB, and (iii) freeing protein resources by decreasing unneeded expression.
results.evaluation: The second reviewer explicitly states 'While they do not reach strong conclusions about how these mutations promote autotrophic growth, they provide some clues, leading to valuable speculation' and 'The authors acknowledge that it will require additional experiments to determine whether the speculated mechanisms are correct.' This indicates the mechanistic interpretations are treated as plausible hypotheses rather than definitively established conclusions.

results.result: The study demonstrates the malleability of metabolism and its capacity to switch trophic modes using only a small number of genetic changes, showing that synthetic autotrophy in E. coli can now be achieved with only a few defined steps.
results.evaluation: The first reviewer explicitly endorses this conclusion, stating the work 'highlight[s] the malleability of E. coli metabolism.' Both reviewers treat this as an important contribution without raising concerns. The first reviewer calls it 'an important follow-up study' and notes it will be 'particularly interesting to synthetic biologists, systems biologists, and metabolic engineers.'

results.result: The crp H22N mutation is located in 'activation region 2' of the protein (an RNA polymerase interaction region) and affects promoter specificity, while the rpoB A1245V mutation is situated within the RNA polymerase core proximal to DNA interaction, with both mutations previously documented in other adaptive evolution contexts.
results.evaluation: The reviewers accept these structural and literature-based characterizations without objection. The second reviewer notes 'The authors have also expanded their description of the crp and rpoB mutations, making it clearer that the effects of these mutations are likely to be distinct, albeit with potential for overlap in function,' indicating acceptance of the structural and functional context provided.

results.result: The authors propose that metabolic rewiring can serve as a temporary 'metabolic scaffold' to direct lab evolution, which can be removed once the desired phenotype is achieved, potentially overcoming the common limitation where evolution deactivates heterologously expressed genes.
results.evaluation: The reviewers do not challenge this conceptual framework. The first reviewer's emphasis on 'the malleability of E. coli metabolism' and the second reviewer's acknowledgment of 'valuable speculation' suggest acceptance of this interpretive framework, even if it represents a conceptual contribution rather than direct experimental validation.

comparisons.comparison: Strong agreement on the core finding that three mutations (pgi, rpoB, crp) are sufficient for autotrophy. Both evaluations rate this as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes the iterative evolution/engineering workflow and reversion experiments, while peer review focuses on the identification of the mutation set. Peer review includes additional claims (C38, C40) about unintentional mutations that OpenEval addresses separately in R10.

Complete agreement on the pgi loss-of-function mechanism. Both evaluations rate this as SUPPORTED and explicitly endorse the mechanistic interpretation. OpenEval provides detailed assessment of enzymatic assays and metabolomics data (C55-C59), while peer review emphasizes the convincing case made for preventing efflux from the autocatalytic cycle. Peer review includes additional claims (C50, C51) not in OpenEval R3.

Agreement on proteomics findings showing effects of crp and rpoB mutations. Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes epistatic effects and incomplete mechanistic understanding, while peer review characterizes the proteomics as providing 'clues' and 'valuable speculation' about mutation roles. Both acknowledge the data quality while recognizing mechanistic gaps.

Perfect claim overlap (C41, C42, C43) on growth characterization and 13C-labeling validation. Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval provides detailed methodological assessment of growth rates, isotopic tracing, and doubling time calculations. Peer review implicitly accepts these validation data without raising concerns.

Partial overlap on NADH/NAD+ measurements (C82-C84) and growth experiments (C79-C81). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval separately evaluates these in R5 and R6, while peer review groups them together as part of the metabolomics/proteomics characterization supporting mechanistic speculation.

Partial overlap on formate-dependent growth experiments (C79-C81). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the interesting phenotype with extended lag time and speculative mechanistic basis. Peer review accepts these data as part of the broader characterization without specific concerns.

Agreement on autotrophic growth without auxiliary knockouts (C44-C47), but different evaluation types. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to the unintentional rrsA mutation creating ambiguity about necessity. Peer review rates as SUPPORTED, focusing on the metabolic scaffold concept (C48) and accepting the demonstration without emphasizing the rrsA caveat.

Perfect claim overlap (C85, C88, C90, C91) on integrative mechanistic model, but different evaluation types. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, noting the model is supported by multiple lines of evidence while acknowledging speculative elements. Peer review rates as UNCERTAIN, explicitly characterizing conclusions as 'valuable speculation' requiring additional experiments.

Perfect claim overlap (C60-C65) on structural and literature context for mutations. Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval characterizes these as contextualizing mutations within known structure-function relationships. Peer review accepts the expanded description of mutation effects and structural locations without objection.

Perfect claim overlap (C95-C98) on metabolic scaffold concept and evolutionary strategy. Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the concept is supported by demonstration that auxiliary knockouts can be removed, with caveats about rrsA. Peer review accepts this conceptual framework as part of the study's interpretive contribution.

Strong overlap (C99, C102) on the main conclusion about metabolic malleability. Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes the synthesis of experimental findings showing sufficiency of three mutations and rapid evolution. Peer review explicitly endorses the conclusion about E. coli metabolic malleability as an important contribution.

Partial overlap (C32, C38, C40) on unintentional mutations and quality control. Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval separately evaluates the identification and testing of unintentional mutations as demonstrating appropriate quality control. Peer review includes these claims within the broader evaluation of the three-mutation finding without separate discussion.

Minimal overlap (C28) on consensus mutation identification from multiple lineages. Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval separately evaluates the logic of distinguishing adaptive from hitchhiker mutations. Peer review includes C28 within the broader evaluation of the mutation identification workflow.

Minimal overlap (C66) on established biochemical knowledge. Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval separately categorizes background knowledge claims (C66-C77) as accurate context rather than novel findings. Peer review includes C66 within the proteomics evaluation without distinguishing background from novel claims.
